title: Detection Strategy for T1542.004 Pre-OS Boot: ROMMONkit
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for T1542.004 Pre-OS Boot: ROMMONkit
summary: This strategy detects ROMMONkit style pre-OS boot tampering, where firmware or boot loader code on a network device is replaced so the device runs attacker controlled instructions before its normal operating system loads. It matters because the change survives reboots, configuration restores and even operating system reinstalls, and it gives the adversary a position below all host based monitoring. Practical detection does not rely on endpoint agents, which cannot see it; it relies on device boot and image integrity records, firmware version and checksum reporting compared with a vendor golden reference, console and remote management session logs, and the authentication records of administrators who reach the boot loader. The main failure is organisational: many networks never collect firmware version or integrity data at all, so the first sign is a device that behaves oddly months later.

beginner.definition: Small boot programs on network hardware start the device before its main software runs. A replacement of that program is called a ROMMONkit. This detection looks for boot code that no longer matches the vendor version. It catches tampering that lives below the operating system.
beginner.whyItMatters: This kind of change survives a reboot, so restarting the device does not remove it. It can hide traffic or survive clean up attempts. Normal security tools on servers never look here. Because the tampering is so persistent, early detection is far cheaper than later removal.
howItWorks: The device reports its boot loader version, firmware release and image checksum when it starts and when it is queried.
Your management platform collects those values and compares them with the approved version for that hardware model.
The detection alerts when a device reports a version or checksum that is not the approved one.
It also looks for entry into the boot loader mode. This usually needs a console or a privileged remote session.
It links that session to an account and a source address, and checks whether a change record exists for it.
Repeated unexplained reboots of the same device raise the priority, because loading new boot code normally needs a restart.
beginner.example: Think of a building where the ground floor is checked by guards each night. Someone replaces the master lock in the basement instead. Every guard on the ground floor sees nothing wrong. Only a check of the basement lock against the official key list shows the change.
takeaways: Pre-OS boot tampering sits below your endpoint and server tools.
Compare device firmware versions and checksums against a known good reference.
Unexplained boot loader sessions and repeated reboots are the earliest clues.

objectives: Describe how firmware and boot loader code sits below the device operating system
Collect and compare device firmware versions and image checksums against a vendor reference
Detect entry into boot loader or recovery modes from console and remote management logs
Correlate boot mode sessions with administrative authentication and change records
Escalate repeated unexplained device reboots for hardware level integrity verification
dataSources: Network device firmware inventory reporting boot loader version, image name and checksum collected by the management platform
Device console and remote management session logs recording entry into boot loader or recovery mode
TACACS+ or RADIUS authentication and command accounting records for privileged administrator sessions
Device boot history logs and syslog records showing repeated or unexpected restarts
Change management records used to validate approved firmware upgrades per device
logic: The detection compares reported boot loader and firmware identity against a known good reference for each hardware model, and treats any unexplained difference as an integrity failure rather than a configuration drift. The fields that must be correlated are the device identifier, the reported boot loader version or image checksum, the time the value changed, and the administrator session that preceded it. Benign changes come with a signed vendor image, an approved change record and a named engineer operating from the management network; malicious changes typically show a checksum that matches no vendor release, a boot loader session from an unusual account or address, or a version that reverts to the original after each reboot, which indicates the tampering is not stored where the operator expects.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Network Device Boot Loader Version Mismatch With Approved Baseline
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     event_type: firmware_inventory
#   filter_approved:
#     boot_version|in: approved_firmware_versions
#     image_checksum|in: vendor_golden_checksums
#   condition: selection and not filter_approved
# level: critical
falsePositives: A staged firmware rollout in which some devices run an older approved release until the next maintenance window
Field replacement units delivered by the vendor with a newer boot loader than the documented baseline
Lab or spare devices that are temporarily attached to the production management network for testing
An interrupted upgrade that leaves the device on its original boot loader while the image inventory is refreshed
tuningNotes: Maintain the approved firmware and boot loader list per hardware model in a reference table, refreshed from vendor advisories, rather than embedding versions in the rule, because version strings change with every release. Baseline every device for thirty days so that known maintenance drift and staging states are captured, and require a matching change record before a mismatch is suppressed. Limit real time alerting to core routers, firewalls and remote access concentrators, since those are the devices whose compromise changes the whole network picture. Restricting the rule to models with published checksums reduces false alerts but leaves older hardware with no checksum coverage, so pair it with boot mode session monitoring on those devices.
